result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.moral_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Build the moral graph of a directed graph: marry the parents, drop the directions. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L50905-L50988){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.moral_graph() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Moral graph](/assets/graphs/moral-graph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: the sprinkler network, a directed graph in which cloudy points to rain and sprinkler, and both rain and sprinkler point to wet grass. Right: moral_graph() marries the two parents of wet by joining rain and sprinkler with a new edge (accent color) and drops every direction, giving an undirected graph with five edges." width="100%"} The moral graph joins every pair of nodes that share a child ("marrying" the parents) and then forgets edge directions. It is the first step of exact inference in Bayesian networks (before triangulation into a junction tree, see `complete_to_chordal_graph()`), because each node and its parents must end up in a common clique, and its separation properties encode the conditional independences of the network. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected graph with the same nodes (IDs, labels and attributes kept), one edge per adjacent pair of the original (parallel and opposite edges merged, weights kept from the first edge) and one unweighted edge per pair of co-parents that were not already adjacent. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Every pair of in-neighbors of every node is joined, $O(\sum_v \deg^-(v)^2)$. Matches NetworkX's `moral_graph` (edges compared as unordered pairs). ## Examples {.doc-examples} The classic sprinkler network: rain and sprinkler are married because both wet the grass: ::: {#a776b938 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["cloudy", "rain", "sprinkler", "wet"]) g.add_edges([("cloudy", "rain"), ("cloudy", "sprinkler"), ("rain", "wet"), ("sprinkler", "wet")]) moral = g.moral_graph() sorted(moral.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['cloudy--rain', 'cloudy--sprinkler', 'rain--sprinkler', 'rain--wet', 'sprinkler--wet'] ``` ::: :::
